newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends quiet U.S. session mixed.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends quiet U.S. session mixed.

text.p: The dollar closed slightly higher against the yen and unchanged versus the mark, keeping within the session's well worn, narrow ranges, dealers said.
After the dollar's dramatic tumble and recovery on Friday, following comments from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, Tuesday's tight range and limited volatility frustrated dealers.
"We've been in a real narrow dollar range today with not a lot of interest outside of the parameters of 1.5520 and 1.5560 marks," said Kevin Lawrie, global manager of foreign exchange at Mellon Bank.

The dollar jumped after the mid-morning release of the National Association of Purchasing Management's latest semi-annual survey, which showed most of its members see better U.S. economic growth in the first half of 1997 than in the second half of 1996.
"The only thing I noticed all day was NAPM caused a tick up in dollar trading," Lawrie said, lamenting a lack of market-moving news and data on Tuesday.
A subsequent release showing a record high U.S. current account trade deficit of $47.96 billion in the third quarter, was less dollar-friendly.
However, dealers said the data was of more interest to academics and that market reaction was muted.
The dollar closed unchanged at 1.5525/35 marks from Tuesday's open but ended slightly higher against the yen at 113.32/42 compared to 113.15/20.
Also dampening the dollar's performance was a bout of nervousness over the future direction of German interest rates ahead of a European Union summit in Dublin this week.

Feeding the speculation was news that foreign policy experts from German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's party were looking for ways to bind Italy into Europe's proposed monetary union without allowing for its full entry at the outset.

This aided the mark against the dollar because the possibility of Italy not being a full-fledged member of the initial union in 1999 would reduce the pressure on Germany to lower its interest rates, dealers said.

"I think people became less convinced this morning that the Bundesbank is going to ease rates to help form one European currency going into 1997," said Mark Gargano, managing director of currency derivatives at First Union National Bank.
"I think the market going into the summit is trading on rumors and expectations," he added.
Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the European Union, will host the bi-annual summit for member nations this Friday and Saturday.
In overnight trade, the dollar eased off session highs against the yen amid talk that Kampo, the giant Japanese postal fund, would start hedging foreign bond risk.

In other trading, the dollar rose to 1.3262/72 Swiss francs from 1.3245/55 at Tuesday's open and gained to Canadian $1.3582/87 from C$1.3557/62. Sterling rose to $1.6535/45 from $1.6497/07, while the Australian dollar ended up at $0.8014/19 from $0.8004/09.
